Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

It is unclear whether anything that happened over the past month will go down in the history books as an “October surprise.” Most of the big events did not seem to move the needle relative to existing issues of affordability, war in Iran, mass deportations, and political chaos. Although President Donald Trump announced an oil deal with Russia and federal agents raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the underlying trends favoring Democrats seemed to hold.

The one possible exception is a late-breaking New York Times story about staffers connected to Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska poised to pull off a possible upset, who were part of a reported secret effort to recruit another Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and split the state’s Republican vote; Dan J. Sullivan now also appears on the ballot alongside the incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation. Although there is nothing illegal about “stacking,” an old partisan tactic, the story will feed the Justice Department’s effort to block the state from certifying the election results if the Republican loses. Whether it will have any broader impact, however, remains unclear.

It is unclear whether anything that happened over the past month will go down in the history books as an “October surprise.” Most of the big events did not seem to move the needle relative to existing issues of affordability, war in Iran, mass deportations, and political chaos. Although President Donald Trump announced an oil deal with Russia and federal agents raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the underlying trends favoring Democrats seemed to hold.

The one possible exception is a late-breaking New York Times story about staffers connected to Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska poised to pull off a possible upset, who were part of a reported secret effort to recruit another Dan Sullivan to confuse voters and split the state’s Republican vote; Dan J. Sullivan now also appears on the ballot alongside the incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation. Although there is nothing illegal about “stacking,” an old partisan tactic, the story will feed the Justice Department’s effort to block the state from certifying the election results if the Republican loses. Whether it will have any broader impact, however, remains unclear.

The ambiguity over the October surprise should not itself be surprising. Since 1980, every election cycle has generated speculation about the possibility of one. The term refers to the emergence of earth-shattering news, whether generated by individuals associated with a campaign or by unfolding events, that could dramatically influence the electorate. It was popularized during the 1980 election, when William Casey, Ronald Reagan’s campaign manager, feared that President Jimmy Carter might announce a breakthrough agreement to free the 52 U.S. hostages being held in Iran before Election Day. No such deal materialized before voters cast ballots. Iran ultimately released the hostages minutes after Reagan was inaugurated in January 1981, a dramatic split-screen moment that has fueled longstanding allegations, never conclusively proven, that members of the Reagan campaign interfered with the negotiations by signaling that Tehran would receive more favorable terms under a Republican administration.

Most anticipated October surprises never occur. As in 1980, the fears usually prove greater than the reality. Even when such surprises have emerged—such as the indictment of former Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger over the Iran-Contra affair days before the 1992 vote or the revelation of George W. Bush’s 1976 drunk driving arrest shortly before the 2000 election—other factors appear to have been more consequential in shaping the outcome.

Sometimes, however, major developments, particularly foreign policy, have significantly altered the political environment in the final weeks of the campaign. One of the most dramatic took place in October 1962, when President John F. Kennedy confronted the Soviet Union over the placement of nuclear missiles in Cuba, about 90 miles from the shores of the United States.

Since Kennedy’s inauguration in 1961, Republicans had attacked the young president as incapable of dealing with the threats posed by the Soviet Union. The spectacular failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in April intensified that criticism. In early June 1961, Kennedy met with Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev in Vienna, and Khrushchev treated the U.S. president with little respect and brazenly intimidated him.

Of all the difficult foreign policy challenges that Kennedy confronted in his first two years of office, few were as explosive domestically as Cuba. Vice President Richard Nixon had been hurt in his 1960 presidential run by the fact that Cuba had fallen to communism on Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s watch in 1959. Meanwhile, Kennedy had successfully positioned himself as more hawkish than Nixon, particularly through claims that a so-called missile gap had left the Soviet Union with a strategic advantage.

Domestic tensions over Cuba escalated in the summer of 1962 as reports of a Soviet military buildup on the island hit U.S. politics. As the debate over Cuba heated up, Democrats anticipated the losses normally suffered by president’s party in midterms. With the exception of Democrats in 1934, such losses had been a constant in political life since the Civil War. The economy added to the party’s worries. The stock market had declined, with the steepest one-day drop since 1929 taking place on May 28, while the president clashed with steel industry executives over price increases. Violent struggles over civil rights were occurring in the Deep South. All of this occurred as much of the president’s domestic agenda, including Medicare, was stalled in Congress. Republicans hoped to reduce the size of the large majorities that Democrats enjoyed in the House and Senate.

Republicans believed that Cuba was a winning issue. Evidence of Soviet activity in Cuba first emerged in August, when a U-2 reconnaissance flight captured images indicating the presence of Soviet military equipment, though the president told reporters that there was no indication of any Soviet combat troops. CIA Director John McCone warned Kennedy that Soviets were likely shipping some sort of missiles into Cuba, but many administration officials dismissed his claims as those of a hardline anticommunist Republican.

Two Republicans, Sens. Kenneth Keating of New York and Homer Capehart of Indiana, spent much of August criticizing Kennedy for ignoring Soviet intervention in Cuba and placing the United States at risk. Keating, who was considering a presidential run at a time when liberal northeastern Republicans remained an influential force within the party, ridiculed the president’s claim that the Soviets were only sending defensive weapons that did not require a response. “Who is to say whether a weapon is offensive or defensive?” Keating asked. “It depends on the direction in which it is aimed.” Capehart was far more conservative than his counterpart, having opposed the liberal internationalism of Presidents Franklin Roosevelt and Harry Truman. In Cuba, however, he demanded force, once asking, “How long will the President examine the situation … until the hundreds of Russian troops grow into hundreds of thousands?”

Worried about the political situation, Kennedy told Secretary of State Dean Rusk and National Security Advisor McGeorge Bundy that he wanted to remain in close contact with Republican leaders, the “key gasbags and others,” to calm the growing storm. On Sept. 7, he also tried to demonstrate his resolve by requesting from Congress stand-by authority to mobilize 150,000 men from the Ready Reserve. Arizona Sen. Barry Goldwater, a right-wing Republican who was preparing to run for president in 1964, was not satisfied. “The American people will not be satisfied with the President’s reiteration of a ‘do nothing’ policy toward Cuba,” he said. Keeping a close eye on Capitol Hill, Bundy reported to the president that “[t]he congressional head of steam on this is the most serious that we have had.”

The crisis broke on Oct. 16, just three weeks before the midterms. U-2 reconnaissance flights, which Kennedy had stepped up earlier in the month, returned with photographs of Soviet missile sites being built in Cuba. Military officials understood that the Soviets could strike the U.S. within minutes. Before seeing the photographs, advisor Kenneth O’Donnell had assured the president that “voters won’t give a damn about Cuba.” After revealing the photographs to O’Donnell, Kennedy said, “You’d better believe it. We’ve just elected Capehart in Indiana and Ken Keating will probably be the next president of the United States.”

After being briefed on the situation, Kennedy formed the Executive Committee of the National Security Council to deliberate over the available options. Its members debated everything from a full-scale military strike to an intensive diplomatic effort. Kennedy pushed back against the hawkish recommendations of military leaders, wary of how quickly the crisis could spin out of control.

On Oct. 22, Kennedy addressed the nation on television to announce his middle ground solution. The U.S. Navy would impose a quarantine around Cuba to prevent additional military material from reaching the island. At the same time, he demanded that the Soviet Union remove the offensive weapons that had already been installed.

From the moment Kennedy made his announcement until Oct. 28, the nation waited with bated breath to see what would happen, terrified that nuclear war might be imminent. After years of school children doing “duck-and-cover” drills in the classroom and suburban families building bomb shelters in case of war, an actual crisis was unfolding. Americans watched anxiously as Soviet ships approached the quarantine line. Those living in dense cities mapped out escape routes and made emergency plans in case of a nuclear attack. Years later, archival material revealed that Soviet commanders in Cuba had been granted authority to deploy certain weapons without direction from the Kremlin.

The first political result of the crisis was to neutralize Cuba as a Republican campaign issue, producing a classic “rally-around-the-flag” effect. Although 8,000 conservative activists gathered at Madison Square Garden to criticize the president for his reluctance to use military force, most Republican leaders vowed to avoid stumping on the issue. At the same time, Kennedy had been on the campaign trail before his address, in part to hide the fact that a major crisis was unfolding.

One day after Soviet forces shot down a U-2 reconnaissance plane over Cuba, killing its pilot, the crisis ended. Through an exchange of letters between Kennedy and Khrushchev, as well as secret talks between Attorney General Robert Kennedy and Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin, the two sides reached an agreement: The Soviets would remove the missiles from Cuba, while the United States would pledge not to invade Cuba. In a secret side agreement, Kennedy vowed that the United States would remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

The second political effect of the crisis was to bolster the standing of Kennedy, and the Democratic Party. The president left the crisis perceived as a highly effective leader on foreign policy—a sharp contrast to the image after the Bay of Pigs—and Republicans had avoided one of the most fraught issues for weeks: The claim that Democrats were “soft on communism,” a staple of GOP rhetoric since the fall of China to communism in 1949, lost some of its force for the time being. Kennedy’s approval rating increased by 13 percentage points, reaching 74 percent.

Democrats did well in the elections, avoiding the normal cycle of loss. They gained four seats in the Senate and only lost a few seats in the House. While Republicans scored some important victories, such as George Romney’s election as Michigan governor, Democrats generally thrived. A new generation of talented liberal senators, including Indiana’s Birch Bayh and South Dakota’s George McGovern, entered the upper chamber, where they would leave their mark over the decade. (Capehart, who was seeking reelection, lost to Bayh.)

Although scholars debate the precise electoral impact of Kennedy’s handling of the missile crisis, one thing is sure: The confrontation dominated the news and boosted Kennedy’s standing in an area where he had been viewed as weak. “It must be assumed that the Democratic party gained rather than lost by its leader’s well-dramatized action,” concluded the chairman of the Republican Congressional Campaign Committee.

The midterm also laid the foundation for even bigger gains in the 1964 election. The neutralization of national security as an effective partisan issue made it more difficult for Goldwater to attack Lyndon Johnson, who became president after Kennedy’s assassination, on this front.

While October surprises have often failed to materialize, there have been moments when unexpected effects dramatically reshape the political playing field. This was the case in 1962.

Today, a consequential October surprise is even less likely to alter the course of an election. Hyperpolarization has rendered much of the electorate resistant to change, even in the face of extraordinary events, such as a pandemic. The fragmentation of the media environment has made it harder for single issues—or even presidents—to command public attention for very long. Meanwhile, the spread of disinformation has made it more difficult for candidates to persuade voters of almost anything. High levels of political disengagement and distrust have also reduced the chances that disaffected citizens will vote. Finally, in both terms, Trump has gone so far to normalize the unpredictable that it is hard for anything to create shock and awe anymore.

Still, history is full of surprises. In early October 1962, very few Americans imagined that the final weeks before the elections would be dominated by a crisis that brought the United States and the Soviet Union to the brink of nuclear war. Sometimes the unpredictable forces of history are the one factor strong enough to break through the political gridlock that constrains the possibility of major change.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

#5985. Don’t Read Too Much Into These Midterms

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Don’t Read Too Much Into These Midterms

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

If there’s one truism in U.S. politics, it’s that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Eggheads like me in Washington might go back and forth on what we believe the American people want from foreign policy, complete with polls that reflect our own opinions. But it is rarely, if ever, the case that foreign policy is a salient enough issue to drive voting behavior.

With his Iran war, however, President Donald Trump has made a foreign-policy choice so destructive and toxic that it has raised the ire of voters—and likely cratered his party’s chances heading into the midterm elections on Tuesday.

If there’s one truism in U.S. politics, it’s that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Eggheads like me in Washington might go back and forth on what we believe the American people want from foreign policy, complete with polls that reflect our own opinions. But it is rarely, if ever, the case that foreign policy is a salient enough issue to drive voting behavior.

With his Iran war, however, President Donald Trump has made a foreign-policy choice so destructive and toxic that it has raised the ire of voters—and likely cratered his party’s chances heading into the midterm elections on Tuesday.

Despite this, we should be cautious about overinterpreting these results. As the horse race for the 2028 presidential election kicks off in the coming weeks, you’ll hear about the ways in which the election is a wholesale rejection of the Trump administration’s foreign-policy choices. This would be an oversimplification. What voters are incensed about is the war with Iran, not necessarily Trump’s broader rejection of the old bipartisan foreign-policy consensus.

Honestly, it’s not clear from polling or focus groups what it is that American voters want from foreign policy, other than perhaps less of it: a reduced role in the world and a policy that focuses on the needs of Americans. For Democrats in particular, then, overreading these midterms as a wholesale rejection of change in foreign policy is a mistake; just because voters have rejected one disastrous foreign-policy choice does not mean that they’re ready to return to the pre-Trump status quo.

There are, in fact, several truisms about U.S. politics that one could apply to this midterm. Parties rarely do well in midterms when they hold the White House, for example; governing is harder than campaigning. Or take lame-duck presidents. Even though they are not on the ballot—and never will be again—midterm results are usually more indicative of voter discontent with the incumbent than how they feel about actual candidates.

And then there’s the truism that voters don’t vote on foreign policy. Certainly, there are marginal cases where foreign-policy opinion can swing votes: Florida’s Cuban exile community, for example, or the marginal impact of Arab American abstentions on Kamala Harris’s electoral chances in Michigan in 2024.

But, in general, though voters will happily express their views on foreign policy when polled, experts say they don’t prioritize it. In 2020, for example, no single foreign-policy issue cracked the top 10 concerns in one Pew Research Center poll; foreign policy overall ranked below the economy, healthcare, Supreme Court appointments, and violent crime as top issues for voters. Perhaps the only time in recent memory where foreign policy took center stage in a midterm election was in 2002, when the “rally around the flag” effect of 9/11 allowed President George W. Bush’s Republican Party to retake control of the Senate.

Yet despite this apparent rule, polling shows that the war with Iran is a top three issue for voters in this election, with 77 percent of respondents in one Gallup poll saying that it’s an extremely or very important issue for them. Gas prices—the most obvious knock-on effect of the conflict for the economy—also rank highly, with 72 percent of voters saying it’s important. (A related foreign-policy issue also cracks the top 10: the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.)

Two reasons for this break from routine explain why the Iran war has resonated so strongly with voters. The first is that the war is not a purely foreign-policy issue. It has made life less affordable for many Americans in concrete and visible ways. Indeed, though some other Trump policies, such as tariffs, have contributed to the higher cost of living faced by Americans today, much of the pain from inflation has been driven by higher energy costs, which jumped only after the start of the war.

Secondly, the Iran war has been a hot-button topic for voters because Trump himself made it one. One of his primary campaign pledges to voters in 2024 was that there would be “no new wars.” He also committed to improving the cost of living; the latter was a priority for many voters following several years of COVID-induced high inflation. The war with Iran is an open and clear betrayal of these promises.

Foreign policy is not the only factor in this election. Trump voters have soured on his tariffs, on the excessively violent immigration crackdowns, and against the blatant corruption of some parts of his administration. Republicans would likely have lost ground in Congress regardless of the war with Iran. But it’s increasingly looking as if they may lose bigger as a result of it.

Despite this, it’s not clear how much we can really learn from these election results. When the polls close on Tuesday night, media attention will quickly turn to the presidential primaries, which are likely to be highly competitive on the Democratic side and at least somewhat competitive among Republicans.

Polls suggest Democrats will retake at least one chamber of Congress. And with tariffs and the Iran war raising prices, foreign policy is a powerful force at the ballot box. What will Democrats do with power? How will the world react? Susan Glasser joins FP Live to analyze the results.

Is the United States destined for a repeat of Jan. 6 every election now?

We can expect that foreign policy—given its high salience in the midterms and the likelihood that the war with Iran will continue for some time yet—will remain a key topic of discussion. If Democrats take the Senate, they may well initiate impeachment hearings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Those hearings will examine not only the Iran war but also U.S. military actions in the Caribbean. Some congressional Democrats are also pushing for a confrontation with Trump over arms for Ukraine.

There will be a tendency, particularly among congressional Democrats, to see these midterm results as voters rejecting Trump’s foreign-policy promises writ large or—more worryingly—as a vote by the public for a return to the pre-Trump foreign-policy status quo. But they would instead be wise to see this more as a single-issue vote: a rejection of the Iran war and of a president who promised one thing and did another.

Americans remain deeply divided about what they want from their foreign policy. Many voters are unhappy with the Trump administration on tariffs, on Iran, on Venezuela, on Trump’s apparent rejection of long-standing U.S. alliances.

At the same time, many of Trump’s discrete policies are not unpopular. Americans generally express support for alliances such as NATO, but a sizable proportion do want Europeans to contribute more to defense; 49 percent of Americans want to cut military aid to other nations. Voters tell pollsters that they disapprove of the shuttering of the U.S. Agency for International Development, but only 17 percent of Americans want to expand humanitarian aid. And in direct contrast to the more hawkish views prevalent in Washington, Trump’s détente with China is popular. Only 40 percent of those polled believe that the United States should actively work to limit the growth of Chinese power.

In short—as the racers climb onto the starting blocks for the 2028 presidential primaries—they would be well advised not to overread the lessons of the midterm elections on foreign policy. Democrats in particular would be wise not to spend the next few years picking fights on issues such as arms to Ukraine, which is only popular with a minority of voters—and only important to a superminority. Instead, candidates and Congress alike would be wise to hold Trump’s feet to the fire on issues that are broadly unpopular with the electorate, such as the Iran war, and even perhaps to co-opt the “America First” language popularized by Trump in his first term.

After all, if there is one lesson we can take from these midterms, it is that voters do not believe that the war with Iran puts Americans first. They want a foreign policy that does.

Emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford

#5984. Can the Nordic Model Save NATO?

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTI PESU is Senior Research Fellow in the Finland and Northern European Security Research Program at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

In August, at Finland’s request, the Swedish government deployed fighter aircraft and a warship to help patrol Finland’s eastern airspace and the Gulf of Finland against Russian air incursions and drones straying from Ukrainian operations. Critically, the Swedish assets involved were placed under Finnish command and followed Finnish rules of engagement. It was the latest example of how Finland and Sweden, the two newest additions to NATO, have made qualitative leaps in defense coordination.

The Nordic countries have expanded regional collaboration significantly in the past four years. Between them, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden now boast a new long-term defense strategy, a cross-border transit area, frequent joint exercises, and unprecedented levels of command integration. In effect, these governments are forming their own regional deterrence cluster: a like-minded group of states deepening military cooperation to strengthen deterrence and, if required, ensure NATO’s broader collective defense.

The Nordic model offers a glimpse of the adaptive solutions that may sustain NATO through uncertain times. Moscow’s appetite for risk is growing; its military buildup and escalating attacks on European infrastructure suggest that Russia constitutes a long-term threat to the alliance. At the same time, the Trump administration is pushing its European allies to take primary responsibility for the continent’s defense. Europeans must therefore deter a more dangerous Russia with less help.

To strengthen their deterrence and defense capabilities, member states along NATO’s extended frontline—and in the Baltic and Black Sea regions, in particular—should build their own regional clusters and foster a strong latticework of bilateral and “minilateral” partnerships with their neighbors. Regionalization remains a taboo subject among most of the alliance’s political leadership; NATO is, after all, a collective defense alliance founded on indivisible security. But regional efforts at the military level will both make NATO more effective and advance the United States’ vision of a more European NATO.

Nordic-style deterrence clusters are thus a win-win. Yet in its erratic, occasionally aggressive approach to Greenland and the North Atlantic, Washington has risked undercutting the very allies that are delivering what it wants. The United States should use the recently signed Greenland deal as a reset to embrace Nordic defense efforts and create incentives for other allies to follow suit.

Nordic defense collaboration took its current institutional form in 2009, when recession-era budgetary constraints pushed the region’s five countries to rethink their defense commitments. Finland and Sweden joined NATO members Denmark, Iceland, and Norway in establishing the Nordic Defense Cooperation, primarily in hopes of cutting procurement costs. NORDEFCO boasted some early wins, including cross-border air force training in the uncongested airspace of northern Finland, Norway, and Sweden. But because NORDEFCO spanned NATO members and nonallied states, bureaucratic hurdles and a lenient threat environment quickly sapped momentum from joint procurement.

Only after Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine did some Nordic countries begin to see cooperation as a security imperative, not just a way to save money. Finland and Sweden launched a no-limits military partnership that included joint wartime planning. And Norway, despite maintaining its NATO-first approach, gradually embraced operational cooperation with its two non-NATO neighbors in times of crisis. By 2020, when the countries signed a trilateral statement of intent, they were conducting extensive joint exercises, sharing intelligence on common threats, and discussing their national defense plans with an eye toward coordinated crisis response.

Any remaining limits on Nordic military cooperation evaporated once Finland and Sweden joined NATO following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The region’s five countries agreed that Moscow posed an urgent security threat to themselves and to Europe as a whole. Even Denmark, which was previously reticent about regional collaboration, warmed to collective defense efforts. In 2023, it joined Finland, Norway, and Sweden in developing the Nordic Airpower Concept, which will give them the ability to fight as one force with their combined 250 advanced fighter aircraft. Denmark has also pledged to contribute personnel to the Swedish-led Forward Land Forces Finland, the NATO battle group that rotates between northern Finland and Sweden. When Denmark served as chair of NORDEFCO in 2024, the five governments also signed NORDEFCO Vision 2030, which outlines their ambition for joint operations that are aligned with both national and NATO defense interests. To support the logistical underpinnings of land force cooperation, the initiative established a seamless, borderless Nordic military mobility corridor.

A division of labor is now emerging: Finland commands regional land operations, Norway hosts the regional headquarters for air operations, and Sweden is becoming the logistics hub and transit area for joint military operations in northern Europe. Denmark, for its part, hosts a regional headquarters for special operations. The Nordic deterrence cluster also functions smoothly within NATO’s collective defense framework. Larger NATO allies—including France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States—routinely operate and exercise in the Nordic space alongside their regional partners and fill capability gaps in areas such as intelligence, reconnaissance, and surveillance. The result is an increase in defense capabilities in NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, which covers the North Atlantic and includes vital sea-lanes, critical undersea infrastructure, and the Arctic and Nordic regions bordering Russian strategic hot spots.

Deterrence clusters could well be the future of NATO’s frontline posture. In addition to NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, NATO has two more regional plans—Center, covering the Baltic states and central Europe, and Southeast, covering Turkey and the Balkans—each with its own operations area and command center network. Governments in these two regions should follow the Nordic example and take the initiative to strengthen their own minilateral ties within the NATO framework.

An obvious starting point is the southeastern Baltic Sea, which sits at the heart of NATO’s Joint Operations Area Center. Although the Baltic states have a shared vulnerability to Russian encroachment, defense cooperation has been modest since they joined NATO, with Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania preferring to rely on extraregional patrons such as the United States. Recent moves, however, suggest that regional collaboration is gathering pace: Estonia and Latvia have jointly procured the IRIS-T air defense system, and all three countries are coordinating their HIMARS rocket systems and building the Baltic Defense Line, a fortification project designed to channel, delay, and block a Russian ground invasion.

But Baltic cooperation would benefit from a more comprehensive minilateral layer resembling NORDEFCO. In practice, this could mean coordinating national defense plans, conducting joint exercises, and sharing missile stocks for air defense systems. It could also entail merging HIMARS launchers for joint fires capability, better integrating national contributions to the Baltic Defense Line, and jointly operating uncrewed vessels to monitor the sea and underwater infrastructure. The aim would be to enable three militaries to fight together as seamlessly as possible, generating a combined power greater than the sum of its parts.

Such a format, if realized, should also involve Poland—an emerging European military powerhouse that currently plays a limited role in Baltic defense. Although Warsaw maintains a relatively robust defense partnership with Lithuania, involving joint exercises and working groups, the two neighbors have previously failed to establish a joint exercise area in the Suwalki Gap, a key strategic corridor and vulnerable supply line connecting the Baltic states to continental Europe. A stronger minilateral framework would create a standing process for joint planning and consultation that could resolve the local objections and divergent strategic priorities that have dogged previous negotiations over the gap.

Within such a framework, Warsaw could reinforce regional defense by connecting its East Shield—Poland’s own program of fortifications, barriers, and surveillance systems along its borders with Russia and Belarus—with the Baltic Defense Line and by contributing ground-based air defenses to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission. The fundamental aim should be to strengthen Poland’s role as a leading security provider in the Baltic region alongside Germany, which is permanently stationing a brigade in Lithuania.

The other frontline arena that would most benefit from a deterrence cluster is the Black Sea region, which sits within NATO’s Joint Operations Area Southeast. Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey have struggled to cooperate because of divergent assessments of the threat posed by Russia. Building minilateral latticework here is clearly harder than in the Nordic or Baltic Sea areas. But in a more European NATO, the rest of the alliance would expect Black Sea allies to contribute more to collective defense, and the conditions for doing so are improving.

The most promising domain for expanded minilateral cooperation is maritime. In July 2024, Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey launched a joint mine-clearing operation, which led to the establishment of a joint mission to protect energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks, and undersea pipelines owned and operated by the three allies. This embryonic naval force could be developed further to cover more ambitious contingencies in the Black Sea, from sea surveillance to the protection of territorial integrity, as the Finnish-Swedish naval task force does in the Baltic Sea.

Air forces are another potentially fruitful area for Nordic-style collaboration, especially as regional militaries grow their capabilities. Bulgaria awaits its F-16s, Romania is set to acquire F-35s, and Turkey, already a potent air power, is seeking readmission to the F-35 program. In 2009, the Nordic air forces began weekly cross-border training, paving the way for today’s cooperation. More frequent exercises among the Black Sea allies would be a logical first step toward enhancing interoperability.

For the Nordics, reaching today’s level of collaboration took more than 15 years. Other frontline regions cannot afford to wait that long. Russia may emerge from the war in Ukraine more capable and less risk averse. Tighter subregional cooperation would not only benefit the security of exposed allies on the frontline by enhancing their capacity to respond together. It would also make NATO’s frontline posture more effective, deterring Russian encroachment deeper into Europe—an aim that allies farther from the frontline should share. Moreover, by strengthening the minilateral latticework, countries close to Russia would enhance their capacity to act together before NATO acted collectively. In extreme circumstances, if the alliance was paralyzed, subregional clusters would offer a hedge, enabling frontline allies to respond together.

The United States, too, has a vested interest in the development of deterrence clusters across NATO’s eastern borderlands. U.S. officials have articulated a vision for “NATO 3.0,” a rebalanced alliance in which Europeans lead their own conventional defense and the United States plays a supporting role, providing extended nuclear deterrence and a few other capabilities. If the Europeans are to assume primary responsibility for their conventional defense, subregional cooperation arrangements—with high interoperability, joint procurement, planning and command capacity, cross-border mobility, and even certain divisions of labor—will be paramount.

Nordic defense cooperation represents the most mature version of such efforts, and the Nordic states have already demonstrated their readiness to work with the United States on Russian-related security threats. Finland and Norway, for instance, have directed their intelligence capabilities toward monitoring what happens on the Russian side of their borders, and Finland lets U.S. signals-intelligence aircraft use its airspace to monitor the Kola Peninsula, where the majority of Russia’s nuclear second-strike capability is concentrated. By preventing Russian dominance in the broader North Atlantic, Nordic cooperation has also advanced the 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy objective of maintaining—in cooperation with allies and partners—favorable balances of power in the world’s key regions.

There is every reason for Washington to treat the Nordic states as exemplary allies and endorse their advancements in regional cooperation. And yet the Trump administration’s approach to the region has been at best incoherent. On the one hand, U.S. officials have commended Nordic efforts to bolster defense spending—Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden are all above or on track to reach three percent of GDP by 2029 and are committed to reaching the Hague target of five percent of GDP by 2035. On the other, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about taking over Greenland, a nightmare scenario for the Nordics that would pit their mutual solidarity against their respective relationships with the United States.

The Greenland agreement that Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk signed in September should encourage the Trump administration to play a larger, more constructive role in Arctic security. So far, Washington has treated defense spending as the key enabler of NATO 3.0. But a European-led alliance also needs allies that can use their growing capabilities as efficiently and seamlessly as possible. If the United States were to encourage and back Nordic-style minilateral latticework in other critical subregions, it would empower a more competent, capable, and commanding NATO 3.0.

The Greenland Deal Proves Self-Reliance Is Not an Option

#5983. Michigan Dem claims Stevens shot down Rogers endorsement rumor hours before turning on El-Sayed

Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., had told her that reports she would support Republican Mike Rogers were "a rumor" and "not true." Stevens endorsed Rogers hours later. (Credit: WJBK)

The decision by Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., to endorse Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers was apparently a sudden change of heart, and tied to the Abdul El-Sayed campaign's stay-away order this weekend.

Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said Stevens told her Saturday night that reports of an impending Rogers endorsement were not accurate.

"It's very hard," Dingell told local FOX 2 on Sunday night. "Haley Stevens told me at midnight last night this was all a rumor and was not true."

DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH

Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens appears alongside GOP rival Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Nov. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Rogers for Senate)

Five hours later, Stevens was standing shoulder to shoulder with Rogers at a Detroit church service.

"She texted me at 7:45, watching you on MS NOW, heart, heart," Dingell continued. "And by the way, I talked to her. Look, I'm just upset. I'm very concerned. It's sad, but I don't want to be distracted anymore."

The Detroit church event was intended to bring unity for El-Sayed's campaign, because Stevens had won the Black vote, but instead, after being told by the Democratic nominee to stay away, she unified with Rogers.

FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY

"We got a phone call this morning and, you know, there's been a lot of unfortunate activity, I think," Rogers told FOX 2 Detroit. "Abdul discarded Haley Stevens, was rude to Haley Stevens, has been rude, I think, to many in the African-American community. At least that's what they're telling me. And I think this just boiled over when he dis-invited her to the campaign event that was supposed to happen today. And basically said don't need you and don't need your supporters."

Rogers welcomed the early November surprise with just two days to go before Tuesday's Election Day in a race that could flip the Democratic Senate seat red and help President Donald Trump's party keep control of the upper chamber.

HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'

"I think she picked up the phone today after having lots of, apparently, conversations with a lot of people and picked up a phone and said, 'Hey, I heard you’re going to church, you want some company?'" Rogers added. "And so that was, I mean, we were very welcome for her, I’m very welcome to have her support."

The unity event became divisive for the former Democratic Senate primary combatants after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blamed Israel for high grocery prices. Stevens' fiancé Jason Turkish, a Democratic donor and Jewish lawyer, said earlier in the week that he was going to vote for Rogers, raising concern from El-Sayed's campaign and other Democrats.

ROGERS OPENS DOOR TO DEMOCRATIC VOTERS AFTER EL-SAYED’S PRIMARY VICTORY: ‘THERE IS STILL HOPE’

El-Sayed’s campaign then asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day to avoid distracting from the race, sources said.

In a social media video, Stevens said, "I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign."

Rogers said Democrats were "veering off into the virulent hate" directed at a group of people, while Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, told Reuters her daughter was concerned about rhetoric she believed frightened constituents.

BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE'

Despite the rift, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens’ endorsement, its second-best fundraising day since the August primary.

Fox News Power Rankings' latest projection rates the race as a Toss Up. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority.

While midterm election history tends to deliver power back to the party in the minority, Trump and Republicans have put added emphasis on retaining Senate control to hold back what is expected to become a Democrat-controlled House.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

Argument: Lula’s Succession Race Starts Now

Since Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise Oct. 25 reelection victory, global attention has focused on his opponent, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio—the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022—promptly fled to the United States, where he declared himself the “leader of Brazil.” The younger Bolsonaro is under criminal investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering.

Flávio’s departure from Brazil will have consequences for the country’s right. But for now, the more intriguing question is about the future of Brazil’s left. Lula turned 81 on Tuesday. Although he is fresh off an electoral triumph, he will need to start cultivating viable successors immediately—a task that he has struggled with in the past.

Since Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise Oct. 25 reelection victory, global attention has focused on his opponent, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio—the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022—promptly fled to the United States, where he declared himself the “leader of Brazil.” The younger Bolsonaro is under criminal investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering.

Flávio’s departure from Brazil will have consequences for the country’s right. But for now, the more intriguing question is about the future of Brazil’s left. Lula turned 81 on Tuesday. Although he is fresh off an electoral triumph, he will need to start cultivating viable successors immediately—a task that he has struggled with in the past.

Lula’s political resilience and longevity are unmatched by most democratically elected politicians. He first ran for president in 1989 and won on his fourth attempt, in 2002. After two presidential terms lasting from 2003 to 2010, a corruption conviction kept him out of the 2018 race that brought Jair Bolsonaro to power. Brazil’s Supreme Court annulled Lula’s conviction in 2021, and he defeated Bolsonaro the following year by less than 2 points. Lula won his fourth term in the contest against Flávio by roughly twice that margin. Since Brazil’s redemocratization in the 1980s, no other politician has been elected president more than twice.

Lula has shown a remarkable ability to adapt to new political realities and change his policy programs without losing his base. In government, he has traditionally moved to the center, building coalitions with parties that share few positions with his Workers’ Party (PT). His first vice president in the early 2000s was a textile mogul who helped assuage concerns among economic elites about Lula’s candidacy. His current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, was the center-right presidential candidate whom Lula beat in the 2006 runoff. Whenever out of power, Lula has returned to lead the left—and occupied that space so that no rival could emerge.

Those who tried to challenge Lula and the PT’s dominance on the left have failed spectacularly. Marina Silva, Lula’s environment minister from 2003 to 2008, left the PT and became a serious presidential contender in 2014 under the banner of the Brazilian Socialist Party. She ran on a platform that combined a progressive social agenda with market-friendly economics.

When polls showed that she was likely to win a runoff against President Dilma Rousseff—Lula’s chosen successor—the PT aired vicious television ads against Silva. Her candidacy never recovered. In 2023, while in office for a third time, Lula brought her back as environment minister.

Ciro Gomes, who served as minister for regional development in Lula’s first cabinet, attempted to run for president in 2010. Yet Lula maneuvered to keep his governing coalition united behind Rousseff, and Ciro’s own party dropped his candidacy. Four years later, the PT drew the Gomes family back in, with Ciro’s brother serving as Rousseff’s education minister. Lula’s strategy has been consistent: contain and weaken the rival, then bring them or their allies back into the fold.

That method has kept Lula at the center of Brazilian politics for four decades. It also deprived the left of anyone who had the national visibility to succeed him. For years, the PT’s best-known alternative candidate was Fernando Haddad, who served as education minister under both Lula and Rousseff and, until March, as Lula’s finance minister. But he has now lost four elections in a row: for reelection as mayor of São Paulo in 2016, for president in 2018, and for governor of São Paulo in 2022 and again this month.

Lula will have to address his succession problem in what is likely to be the most challenging of his four terms. Starting in February, the Bolsonaro-backed Liberal Party will hold 121 of 513 seats in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies and 28 of 81 seats in the Senate, making it the largest caucus in both. That will make it hard for Lula to pass legislative priorities or get Supreme Court nominees confirmed.

According to the International Monetary Fund, Brazil’s fiscal deficit will be close to 8 percent of GDP this year. Gross public debt stands at above 80 percent of GDP, by the central bank’s measure—and at above 90 percent by the fund’s assessment. That leaves very little room for the spending increases that Lula promised during his campaign. U.S. tariffs on Brazil remain in force, and with the Strait of Hormuz still under threat, oil prices climbed above $115 a barrel this month, feeding energy costs and inflation across Latin America.

Lula is thus bound to face high public rejection rates from day one. And since, as an incumbent, he won’t have the honeymoon period that recently elected presidents usually enjoy, he risks becoming a lame duck early. A president governing under these constraints has every incentive to keep power close. Yet Lula’s political legacy—and the left’s capacity to remain competitive without him—now depend on him doing what he has avoided throughout his career: letting others grow and, ideally, outshine him.

Lula’s one previous attempt at developing a successor was not encouraging. Choosing Rousseff to run for the presidency in 2010 was perhaps the gravest political error of his career. Rousseff had previously served as energy minister in Lula’s first government and later became his chief of staff. But she had never run for office, lacked the skills to work with Congress, and pursued an interventionist economic program that helped produce a deep recession.

Brazil’s GDP fell 3.5 percent in 2015 and 3.3 percent in 2016, its worst two-year stretch in more than a century. Rousseff was impeached that year. After a period of commodity boom-fueled growth and optimism, the economic downturn led to widespread discontent and ultimately opened the way for Bolsonaro to win in 2018.

Lula is hardly alone in mishandling a potential successor. Former U.S. President Joe Biden tasked Vice President Kamala Harris with addressing the root causes of migration from Central America, an assignment with few chances of visible success. That made it harder for her to be competitive when he withdrew from the 2024 race.

Now, Lula should build a bench instead of anointing an heir. There are several younger politicians in the PT and allied parties who could become nationally known and tested over the next several years.

The most obvious candidate is Rafael Fonteles, the 41-year-old governor of Piauí. Elected in 2022 at the age of 37, he became the youngest governor in the state’s history after serving as its finance secretary from 2015 to 2022. He belongs to the PT’s more market-friendly wing. This month, he was reelected with 70.9 percent of the vote. Piauí now has the lowest homicide rate of the nine states in Brazil’s northeast. After losing the first round of the presidential race to Flávio, Lula put Fonteles in charge of his campaign’s communication—which markedly improved as a result.

If Fonteles left the governorship, Lula could make him finance minister, a post now held by Dario Durigan, who replaced Haddad in March. The ministry would expose Fonteles to the national and international business communities and increase his name recognition. The downside of serving as finance minister is that the next four years will require the government to make unpopular economic decisions, and Lula would have to make sure that whoever gets the job does not absorb all the political cost.

The Foreign Ministry is an alternative: Fonteles is known to have a keen interest in international affairs and has actively sought to attract foreign investors to Piauí. Making him foreign minister would carry fewer risks and be an opportunity to present a younger, progressive Brazilian leader to the world.

Camilo Santana, a two-term governor of the state of Ceará and former education minister, leads the PT in the Senate. At 58 years old, he was the political coordinator of Lula’s runoff campaign. João Campos, 32, of the Brazilian Socialist Party, and Renan Filho, 47, of the centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement, both lost governor’s races this month. Ministry posts would keep both in national politics; Lula himself has mentioned Campos as a possible candidate for 2030. Durigan is in his early 40s, but as a technocrat, he lacks a base of his own.

Giving key ministerial posts to all these contenders would be difficult. Countless allies of the president—including Haddad; former PT President and Federal Deputy Gleisi Hoffmann, who until this year was Lula’s chief negotiator with Congress; and Rio de Janeiro Mayor Eduardo Paes—lost their election races and may expect Lula to give them positions in his cabinet.

Rather than specifically aiming to nurture leaders for the presidential contest in 2030, Lula should view his succession strategy as a long-term project to keep the PT competitive. Given pervasive anti-incumbency sentiment and little hope for sufficient economic growth to offset it, the right is favored to win Brazil’s presidency four years from now—particularly since the scandal-ridden Bolsonaro family appears to have exited the political scene. Unless a new generation of left-wing leaders can use Lula’s final presidential term to gather executive experience, progressive forces risk being the underdogs for several electoral cycles.

Whoever emerges as Lula’s successor will inherit a party that is difficult to manage and that many voters reject outright. In a March Ipsos-Ipec survey of Brazilians, 27 percent cited the PT as their preferred party, and 37 percent said they would never vote for the party.

The PT is also split between a hard-left wing and a social-democratic one. The party’s relationship to Venezuela under former President Nicolás Maduro provided a vivid example. Hoffmann, who led the party from 2017 to 2025, attended Maduro’s 2019 inauguration and described the country’s 2018 presidential vote as legitimate—well after Maduro had become authoritarian. She and Haddad, a leading member of the social-democratic camp, clashed over the trip.

A future candidate will have to constantly manage these tensions without being seen as flip-flopping or opportunistic. But Lula must give them the space to grow. Unless he provides a new generation with the opportunity to gain national and international visibility, the Brazilian left is bound to become an underdog.

Oliver Stuenkel is a senior fellow in the Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington, D.C., and an associate professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo. X: @OliverStuenkel

#5980. The Limits of China’s Self-Sufficiency

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

JOEL WUTHNOW is a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a co-author of China’s Quest for Military Supremacy. The views expressed here are his own.

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

When assessing the probability of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait, analysts tend to focus on a few obvious risks that China would face—namely, military defeat, economic slowdown, and restricted oil and technology imports. All of these are important, but an equally significant vulnerability is often left off the list: China’s reliance on soybean imports.

Beijing recognizes this liability. At the 20th Party Congress, in 2022, Chinese leader Xi Jinping identified “ensuring the security of food, energy resources, and critical industrial supply chains” as issues essential to national security and social stability. Food security, conspicuously listed first, is an especially sensitive issue for China’s 1.4 billion inhabitants: roughly 15 percent of the country’s population today was alive during the 1959–61 famine, which resulted in an estimated 30 million deaths.

As with technology and oil, Beijing has tried to limit its dependence on soybeans by building up stockpiles and diversifying its sources. But because soybeans are a fragile foodstuff, there is only so much China can do. Beijing can support a war effort, therefore, for only as long as the Chinese public could put the People’s Liberation Army’s success above its nutritional needs. And the key for deterring Chinese leaders from starting a conflict is to convince them that a domestic crisis would arrive sooner than any battlefield victory.

Disruption to critical imports is one of the most powerful deterrents to China’s use of force, and it’s a threat that the Chinese government has spent decades working to counter. The specter of a foreign blockade in the Strait of Malacca, through which most of Chinese oil imports pass, has worried Chinese leaders since at least 2003, when Chinese leader Hu Jintao warned about the risk of major powers’ interference creating a “Malacca dilemma” for China’s energy security. Beijing, however, has stockpiled massive reserves of oil, which it could complement in a crisis by increasing imports of Russian oil and, as Moscow has done, building up a sanctions-evading shadow fleet to transport oil from the Middle East.

Access to foreign technology is a newer but just as important concern, and China is similarly stockpiling critical components, such as chips. It is also having success in developing local alternatives. Beijing has already pulled ahead in some sectors, such as solar and battery manufacturing, or it is working to close the gap in others, as in semiconductors.

But Beijing has fewer options when it comes to self-sufficiency in food. Domestic production of staple grains—such as wheat, rice, and corn—accounts for more than 90 percent of consumption in these categories, but China remains dependent on foreign producers for other important foodstuffs, including soybeans, beef, and barley. Between 2000 and 2020, the share of China’s food supply provided by imports grew from six percent to 34 percent, and analysts predict it to increase to 41 percent by 2030. Part of this growth comes from the country’s economic development; as people become wealthier, their diets diversify, and they are no longer satisfied eating only grains. Between 1962 and 2024, meat as a percentage of the typical Chinese diet increased by a factor of 18.

This is where the central role of soybeans comes in. The legume provides a complex array of proteins in animal feed that other food sources and synthetic amino acids cannot replicate. Without it, livestock herds in China would shrink, thereby threatening domestic meat and dairy supplies. Soybean oil is also the most used cooking oil in China, making up nearly half the market. Alternatives, such as palm and rapeseed oils, are also mostly imported and face the same risks of maritime disruption, offering little relief.

China has invested a great deal in securing and, when possible, diversifying its access to foreign food sources. In 2013, a Chinese company bought Smithfield Foods, the United States’ largest pork producer. And state-owned enterprises such as COFCO International, a branch of China’s largest food and agriculture company, are buying farms and building logistical infrastructure in major agriculture-producing countries, such as Argentina and Brazil, which allows them to buy directly from farmers. Such direct investments provide a buffer against price volatility, giving Beijing more control over the volume and cost of supplies at their source. China has also steadily increased its own domestic meat production, which accounts for more than 90 percent of China’s demand. But such efforts do little to mitigate the effects of disruptions in maritime shipping—especially of soybeans, which is a supply chain that is fragile even in peacetime.

The central rub is that China has no choice but to import its soybeans. There is not enough arable land in China to both expand soybean cultivation and sustain self-reliance in staple grains. (Soybeans are also a much less efficient crop than corn or wheat in China’s arid north, making this tradeoff the economical choice.) But the countries that grow and export soybeans are almost all in the Western Hemisphere, which presents even more logistical challenges. When the trade war between the United States and China broke out in 2018, for instance, Beijing limited its U.S. soybean imports from 40 percent to about 20 percent of its supply, making up the difference with increased imports from Brazil. But Brazil’s poor infrastructure and frequent natural disasters make its harvest more susceptible to failure than the U.S. harvest. In 2024, one Brazilian state lost a quarter to a third of its soybean harvest because of flooding.

U.S. and Brazilian ports are also about as far from China as they could be. Brazil’s Santos port, for example, is more than 10,000 miles from Guangzhou, which takes 45 days to ship. Because of soybeans’ sensitivity to humidity, this distance means that ships often arrive in China with rotten cargo. For similar reasons, the legume is also difficult to stockpile. Unlike rice and wheat reserves, which Beijing claims could last for years, soybean reserves are smaller and must be replaced more frequently. Chinese stockpiles might be able to last only a few months if its imports were cut off. Although China has been experimenting with bioengineered supplements in an effort to reduce the amount of soybeans in animal feed, rising food demand is offsetting any gains. In other words, its dependence on soybean imports is only continuing to grow.

The outbreak of war between China and the United States would pose existential threats to this supply chain. In the most extreme scenario, the U.S. military could block shipments from the Western Hemisphere to China, which would take away most of the country’s soybean imports. China has no naval bases or forward forces in Latin America that could counter these efforts.

But China’s food supply chains would suffer from disruption even without a U.S. embargo or blockade. Any war in the Pacific would bring with it massive risk premiums for maritime shipment insurance that might cause shipping firms to balk. Such an effect has already been on display for shipping in the Red Sea, where Houthi missile threats have caused insurance costs to skyrocket since 2024. A war in the Pacific could be far more intense and costly because it would involve major navies, and ships could not route around the danger zone, making the long-haul journey from Brazil financially ruinous for many companies.

Beijing could, in theory, offer sovereign guarantees to offset firms’ insurance premiums. Even then, the firms transporting soybeans, most of which are owned by U.S. and allied country parties, might cease transporting products to China to avoid abetting a hostile regime, to steer clear of dangers that would put their employees at risk, and to head off possible future exposure to sanctions for doing business with the country.

Chinese analysts believe that China could circumvent some of these risks by using its own commercial fleet. Although this fleet has impressive capacity during peacetime—the Chinese shipping giant COSCO owns 468 dry bulk carriers—in wartime it would be stretched thin, facing demands to help move construction materials, industrial supplies, and foodstuffs for the People’s Liberation Army and to transport critical military materials such as coal and iron ore. Even available ships would likely lack personnel with the training needed to keep soybeans fresh during the long journey. And if ships tried to avoid the most dangerous sea-lanes, trips could take even longer, surpassing the 40 days that soybeans can be safely stored. Cargo might arrive rotten, if it arrived at all.

A war in the Pacific would not trigger an immediate food crisis in China. In the shorter term, the government could manage reduced imports by releasing supplies of soybeans, frozen pork, and other staples from state reserves. It could also reduce the minimum soybean inclusion rates for animal feed, which would slow livestock growth and cut meat output but which would be workable for a time. A few months of a managed crunch, however, is a best-case scenario. More likely is that panic buying and shipping disruptions would drain reserves faster than planned, turning a manageable shortfall into rising prices and visible shortages within months.

There is reason to believe, for instance, that Chinese stockpiles might not provide the short-term security they purport to. Over the last decade, local government warehouses meant to store emergency food supplies have been found empty or filled with rotten supplies, largely because of corruption. This not only calls into question how much extra food China truly has but also undermines public confidence in the government. In the case of a conflict, citizens conscious of the long-term disruption to come would begin panic buying and hoarding supplies. Whatever reserves do exist would eventually run out, with members of the elite likely being prioritized.

If the conflict dragged on, the situation would become increasingly dire. Agricultural producers, especially small farms, would be forced to cull their herds. Poultry, which requires especially high soybean content in its feed, would be the first casualty, which would then threaten the egg supply. Pork would be next. Cooking oils would grow scarce and expensive, making it difficult for restaurants and households to function. Eventually, public patience would wear thin: hoarding, protests over prices and shortages, and local officials diverting supplies could put mounting pressure on Beijing to end the war.

Unlike China’s vulnerabilities in energy or technology, the fragilities of the food system are endemic. If a conflict were to break out in the Pacific, the United States would not need to institute a blockade against China’s agricultural supplies or gather an international coalition to sanction China’s soybean imports. Soaring insurance costs and ship owners’ reluctance to sail into a war zone would be enough to squeeze the flow, and the Chinese government would have little recourse to stop it.

If Chinese leaders believed that they could achieve victory quickly and with few shots fired, they might take the bet. Deterrence, then, will require convincing them that they cannot. The United States, Taiwan, and other governments should invest in drones, rebuild munitions stockpiles, and ramp up messaging to China that a long, drawn-out conflict is likely. As long as China’s leaders believe that a war would be indecisive in its early stages, the threat of domestic crisis would be a powerful reason not to start one.

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

#5979. Trump takes midterm campaign blitz to historic stage for grand finale before Election Day

Trump supporters spoke with Fox News Digital at the president's rallies in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, about rising costs, the country's future and what's driving their votes ahead of the midterms.

President Donald Trump is set to deliver his closing midterm campaign message Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., capping a weekslong campaign blitz that has taken him across more than 20 states as Republicans fight to maintain control of Congress in Tuesday's elections.

Trump is scheduled to speak at 2 p.m. ET and participate in nine tele-rallies throughout the day, following in-person campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday.

The president has made 30 in-person political appearances since August, including more than 27 rallies in October, with a longtime adviser who has joined him on the road offering a behind-the-scenes look at the travel, logistics and memorable moments along the way.

LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP IS DEFYING MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS HE BARNSTORMS COUNTRY

President Donald Trump shakes hands with former professional boxer Mike Tyson after he was introduced during an election rally at the Oncenter on October 9, 2026, in Syracuse, New York. Trump is in New York campaigning for local Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Alex Bruesewitz, a senior adviser to Trump's 2024 presidential campaign who has accompanied him on roughly 10 to 15 trips in recent weeks, told Fox News Digital that organizing rallies for a sitting president presents challenges far different from those of a traditional campaign.

"It's actually much different than the campaign," Bruesewitz said. "When you're doing an event moving the current president of the United States, the logistics that go into it are nuts."

The operation requires extensive coordination among White House staff, Republican operatives, campaign aides and advance teams, with the White House Office of Political Affairs, Office of Public Liaison and Republican National Committee all playing roles, according to Bruesewitz.

"President Trump will continue crisscrossing the country with unmatched energy and enthusiasm to deliver a simple message: with Republicans in control of Congress, Americans can expect safer streets, lower taxes, secure borders, and energy dominance," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS

Nicki Minaj pledged her continued support for President Donald Trump during a Michigan campaign rally, telling the president she would back him again if he sought another term. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

The demanding schedule has also produced some memorable moments aboard Air Force One.

Bruesewitz recalled one particularly exhausting West Coast trip that left him sleeping aboard the presidential aircraft at 4 a.m.

"I had a picture of me sleeping on the Air Force One at 4 a.m. [that] ended up somehow in the group chat of all the congressional first spouses," he recalled.

The photograph drew messages from lawmakers' wives surprised by how exhausted he appeared.

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

President Donald Trump waves as he leaves the stage following a campaign rally at Freeman Coliseum on Oct. 7, 2026, in San Antonio, Texas. Trump visited the state to campaign for Republican candidates, including Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton, ahead of the November midterm elections. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Despite the long hours, Bruesewitz described an atmosphere reminiscent of Trump's 2024 campaign, with staffers moving from one event to the next and the president maintaining a packed schedule.

And while the president remains focused on official business and preparing his remarks during flights to campaign stops, Bruesewitz said the mood aboard Air Force One shifts considerably on the way home.

On return flights, staffers unwind with music and football, including a recent Green Bay Packers game that Bruesewitz, a devoted fan of the team, watched aboard the presidential aircraft.

PRESIDENT TALKS 'TRUMP OCEAN,' TRADES JOKES WITH TENNESSEE CROWD AS KID ROCK KICKS OFF SPRAWLING RALLY

People attend a rally with U.S. President Donald Trump at Lubbock Memorial Civic Center on October 27, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The campaign stops have also featured appearances by high-profile celebrities, including boxing legends Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield and rapper Nicki Minaj.

Bruesewitz recalled escorting Tyson to his seat after the boxing legend arrived at an event in New York, drawing excited reactions from attendees who recognized him.

SKY-HIGH GAS PRICES AREN'T SHAKING TRUMP'S MAGA FAITHFUL IN OIL COUNTRY AS SUPPORTERS WARN OF BIGGER THREAT

President Donald Trump walks up to the podium as he arrives to speak at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026. (Matthew Reidy/Fox News)

But one of Bruesewitz's favorite moments came during a recent stop in Port Huron, Michigan, where Minaj joined Trump for an appearance that drew a packed arena despite competing with a Detroit Lions football game.

Bruesewitz said the stop was particularly memorable because many attendees were seeing Trump in person for the first time.

"You could see and sense the enthusiasm of the attendees in the crowd," he said. "They were excited about Nicki going, but they were also just so pumped to be able to see the president in person."

TRUMP'S MAGA FAITHFUL SEND WARNING TO REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF HIGH-STAKES MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Rapper Nicki Minaj joined President Donald Trump onstage during a Republican campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. (2026 Getty Images)

The final stretch also brought a late shift in Trump's campaign schedule, with in-person stops in Kansas and Iowa reinstated for Sunday after initially being scrapped in favor of tele-rallies aimed at reaching voters across nearly 20 states.

After weeks of travel, packed arenas and a demanding schedule aboard Air Force One, Trump's campaign operation is set to close Monday with an appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a rapid-fire series of tele-rallies as Republicans make their final appeal to voters ahead of Election Day.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

#5978. A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

Argument: A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper
